payload.author: zanieb
payload.body:
This sounded familiar so I pulled some history with Codex, I think there's a bunch of nuance we'll need to consider here:

- #1902 established that authorization from the initial HEAD must carry into range requests.
- [#2025](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/2025), [#3255](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/3255), and [#2843](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/2843) found that some indexes redirect HEAD and GET to different presigned S3 URLs. A URL signed for HEAD returns 403 when reused for GET.
- Consequently, in https://github.com/prefix-dev/async_http_range_reader/pull/16 we explicitly changed the reader to “always use requested URL, rather than response URL (see also https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/3460).
- #14126  later introduced uv’s manual redirect wrapper so redirect requests rerun authentication middleware. The underlying `reqwest` client has redirects disabled, and converting the wrapper into the `ClientWithMiddleware` accepted by `AsyncHttpRangeReader` drops that wrapper. This appears to be the actual regression encountered here.
- https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/7226 amplifies the effect: once a range failure is classified as unsupported, uv records that capability for the index and stops range-prefetching there.
- #18998 reports essentially the same GAR shape
- Since https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/1792, the fallback streams until it finds METADATA; it does not necessarily download the entire wheel to disk, though it may consume most of one.

payload.author: konstin

I talked about that with @.oconnor663 some time ago and we noticed that the main problem is that hardlinks use the permissions of the underlying file. There's two ideas that come to mind:

* Separate bucketing for executable vs. non-executable, or making the executable bit part of the hash (either part of input or XOR it in or something)
* Store the file with the executable bit and only copy when the stored copy is wrong. For our examples, it is highly unlikely that there is another rust binary around in the cache so having it in the cache with the executable bit is almost always correct.

payload.author: charliermarsh
payload.body: Yeah, I have tried both of those. https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21327 (prior PR) does the first option, this PR undoes it because I wanted to pipeline the persistence to the `files-v0` store with the extraction from the zip. But we don't know the executable bit until we read the central directory at the _end_. So we'd need to either read the central directory upfront, or "guess" the executable mode when we persist and then correct after-the-fact.

| Wheel | Cache | Parent median | Optimized median | Change (95% CI) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| AnyIO 4.9.0 | cold | 90.4 ms | 93.4 ms | +3.39% (+2.87% to +3.86%) |
| AnyIO 4.9.0 | warm | 29.9 ms | 30.3 ms | +1.14% (-1.08% to +3.85%) |

| NumPy 2.2.6 | cold | 314.1 ms | 326.5 ms | +3.95% (+3.24% to +4.82%) |
| NumPy 2.2.6 | warm | 62.5 ms | 62.7 ms | +0.28% (-0.55% to +1.25%) |
| PyTorch 2.7.1+cpu | cold | 2982.6 ms | 3072.9 ms | +3.03% (+0.98% to +5.18%) |
| PyTorch 2.7.1+cpu | warm | 404.0 ms | 403.1 ms | -0.21% (-0.72% to +0.11%) |

Before this optimization, the measured cold regressions were +4.02% for AnyIO 4.9.0, +19.41% for SymPy 1.14.0, +12.75% for NumPy 2.2.6, +15.30% for PyTorch 2.7.1+cpu.

**All eight median regressions are below 5%.** The PyTorch cold 95% interval still reaches 5.18%, so its upper bound is not below 5%. Every other upper bound is below 5%.

We retained all 1,860 measured installs, including outliers, and combined every confirmation run for this candidate. Cold measurements have 360 paired rounds for AnyIO, 120 each for SymPy and NumPy, and 90 for PyTorch; warm measurements have 60 paired rounds per wheel. Baseline/candidate order alternates, with three warmups per case. Intervals use a paired percentile bootstrap of the ratio of medians with 10,000 resamples.

These measurements ran on Linux/ext4, an AMD EPYC-Milan VM pinned to eight CPUs, with Python 3.12.13. Both binaries use Rust 1.98.0 and the same `profiling` profile (optimized, no LTO). Each sample installs one pinned local wheel offline, without dependencies or bytecode compilation, using hardlinks into a fresh virtual environment. payload.author: charliermarsh
payload.body:
Okay, I experimented with a bunch of alternatives to try and make this more performant:

- Store all files as non-executable, and then apply executable flags at install-time (https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21334, https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/pull/21333). This would allow us to hardlink into `files-v0` while we unzip. Unfortunately, it also means we have to _copy_ every executable that we want to install, since hardlinks share a mode. Ultimately, this was a bit tradeoff -- it was slower!
- Pre-fetching the central directory so that we can determine whether a given file is executable at extraction-time. (As-is, we only get the central directory _after_ we've unzipped, so we don't know if a file is executable until _after_ it's been extracted.) This also turned out to be slower because we have additional overhead from making more HTTP requests.

I also considered something like "guess whether a file is executable" during extraction (and then, if we're wrong, copy it and change the mode after unzipping). I guess this could end up being more performant, but I wasn't very happy with the heuristics.

Ultimately, I think what we have here is good.

payload.author: konstin
payload.body:
Using `in` and `not in` operators with version fields has problems where it doesn't do what it appears to: In your example `python_version in "3.8,3.9,3.10"`, Python 3.1 matches too! It's inconsistent with regular python version specifiers, which don't have `in`/`not in` operators, and so we have since deprecated that syntax (https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/dependency-specifiers/, https://discuss.python.org/t/spec-change-bugfix-dependency-specifiers-simplification-pep-508/105203):

> For Version fields, the comparison operations are defined by the [Version specifier specification](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/version-specifiers/#version-specifiers) when either both the marker field value and the user supplied constant can be parsed as valid version specifiers or the === arbitrary equivalence comparison operator is used. When an operator other than === is used, publishing tools SHOULD emit an error if the user supplied constant cannot be parsed as a valid version specifier, index servers MAY disallow uploads containing such environment markers, while locking and installation tools MAY either emit an error or else fall back to String field comparison logic if either the marker field value or the user supplied constant cannot be parsed as a valid version specifier. Note that in and not in containment checks are NOT valid for Version fields and publishing tools SHOULD emit an error, index servers MAY disallow uploads containing such environment markers, while locking and installation tools MAY treat them as always being False.

I appreciate the effort, but I'd rather leave this as-is and not extend support for it. (We're kinda already supporting too much of it)

> Any advice about the performance regression? I could try for a regex but that would be a larger refactor. I am actually pretty shocked that this would decrease a run by 10% since it's one extra check, and also the CPU pipeline should effectively be able to guess which side of the branch to take. Perhaps the benchmark is not as reliable?

That one looks like a flake, your change shouldn't affect the unzipping performance; It would likely go away on a rerun, that one's not on your change.

The two Windows shards were my tests, now fixed in `715fc88`.

Both assert the `--offline` git error text, which the Windows runners never reach: they fail earlier with

```
could not execute process `[BIN]/git.exe init` (never executed)
This version of %1 is not compatible with the version of Windows you're running.
```

so the harness's bundled `git.exe` does not run there and uv's offline check never fires. The fix itself is platform independent, only the assertion was not, so the tests are now `#[cfg(not(windows))]`, matching `tool_run_csv_with` nearby.

Happy to assert on something portable instead if you would rather they ran everywhere.

The problem with keeping them in the integration tests is we could regress and not notice because the filesystem happened to order things in a way that doesn't trigger a failure case.

payload.author: jjhelmus
payload.body:
I was able to reproduce the original issue in #3578 using an older version of PyTorch, specifically 1.13.0. This uses the latest uv and manually removes the symlink prior to install to simulate the proposed change.

reproduce.sh
``` bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

workdir="${WORKDIR:-/tmp/torch-lib64-reproducer}"
mkdir -p "$workdir"
cd "$workdir"

if ! command -v uv >/dev/null; then
  curl -fsSL https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh -o install-uv.sh
  env UV_INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin UV_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 sh install-uv.sh
fi

uv --version
uv venv --python /usr/bin/python3 uv-env
unlink uv-env/lib64
python3 -m venv --without-pip venv-env

for env in uv-env venv-env; do
  uv pip install --python "$workdir/$env/bin/python" torch==1.13.0
done

echo "=== uv: expected failure ==="
if "$workdir/uv-env/bin/python" -c 'import torch'; then
  echo "Unexpected: import torch succeeded under uv"
  exit 1
fi

echo "=== venv: expected success ==="
"$workdir/venv-env/bin/python" -c 'import torch; print(torch.__version__)'
```

Run with:
``` shell
❯ docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$PWD/reproduce.sh:/reproduce.sh:ro" \
  rockylinux:9 bash /reproduce.sh
```

Results
```   
downloading uv 0.12.3 x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
installing to /usr/local/bin
  uv
  uvx
everything's installed!
uv 0.12.3 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)
Using CPython 3.9.18 interpreter at: /usr/bin/python3
Creating virtual environment at: uv-env
Activate with: source uv-env/bin/activate
Using Python 3.9.18 environment at: uv-env
Resolved 9 packages in 1.15s
... <snip> ...
=== uv: expected failure ===
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/tmp/torch-lib64-reproducer/uv-env/lib64/python3.9/site-packages/torch/__init__.py", line 191, in <module>
    _load_global_deps()
  File "/tmp/torch-lib64-reproducer/uv-env/lib64/python3.9/site-packages/torch/__init__.py", line 153, in _load_global_deps
    ctypes.CDLL(lib_path, mode=ctypes.RTLD_GLOBAL)
  File "/usr/lib64/python3.9/ctypes/__init__.py", line 374, in __init__
    self._handle = _dlopen(self._name, mode)
OSError: libcublas.so.11: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
=== venv: expected success ===
1.13.0+cu117
```

PyTorch added logic to manually search for cuDNN and cuBLAS to avoid this issue (pytorch/pytorch#90426). This logic is included in PyTorch 1.13.1 and newer which likely explains why these work without the symlink.

More generally, Python distributions should not assume that files installed by another package are located at a predictable relative paths. The distributions may be split across purelib and platlib, user and global site-packages, or other sys.path entries. Nevertheless, retaining the symlink provides compatibility with distributions that make this assumption.

A pragmatic approach could be to retain the symlik for environments with Python versions earlier than 3.15 and omit it for Python 3.15 and newer. That would preserve compatibility where needed while matching the behavior of venv.

The speedup is great, but I want to note two concerns:

PGO has a large effect on performance that we currently don't cover neither codspeed nor in profiling builds. It's easy to do optimizations that are replaced by PGO or that show different performance with PGO. That includes subcommands and configurations not in the training set: They currently seem to be the same speed or slightly faster, though it's way less clear and a lot harder to reason about performance. A quick benchmark shows vastly different results based on the subcommand (which in fairness may be IO limits in the `uv cache` case):

| Command | Baseline | PGO | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `uv cache clean` | 24.90 ms | 24.75 ms | −0.9% |
| `uv cache clean <package>` | 13.62 ms | 13.83 ms | +1.7%, not significant |
| `uv cache prune` | 12.30 ms | 12.38 ms | +1.2%, not significant |
| `uv cache prune --ci` | 22.08 ms | 21.84 ms | −0.2% |
| `uv lock --check` | 17.03 ms | 15.74 ms | **−8.2%** |
| `uv add` | 42.06 ms | 39.12 ms | **−7.1%** |
| `uv remove` | 34.01 ms | 30.82 ms | **−8.0%** |
| `uv tree` | 15.94 ms | 14.90 ms | **−6.9%** |
| `uv build --wheel` | 20.47 ms | 19.69 ms | **−4.5%** |
| `uv python list` | 70.67 ms | 63.49 ms | **−9.8%** |
| `uv pip compile` | 23.08 ms | 20.63 ms | **−10.2%** |

PGO builds are much slower. The initial instrumented build is almost twice as slow as a regular release build, which limits iteration when doing profiling. If we're accepting much slower compile times, we should also consider other settings such as `codegen-units = 1`.

payload.author: teamleaderleo
payload.body:
Okay! I reworked this around a runtime capability check. It’s a little more complicated, but the alternatives I tried each seemed to miss a requirement.

I first tried falling back after a failed protected call:
```sh
realpath -- "$0" 2>/dev/null || realpath "$0"
```
That doesn’t work with BusyBox. It treats `--` as another pathname, so the first call can resolve `$0` and still fail because the `--` path doesn’t exist. The fallback then leaves the same path in the command substitution twice:
```text
/path/to/script
/path/to/script
```
I also considered making each relative operand option-safe by prefixing it with `./`:
```sh
case "$0" in
    /*) realpath "$0" ;;
    *)  realpath "./$0" ;;
esac
```
That approach can change which file gets resolved.

For example:
```text
Current directory:
    /tmp
PATH lookup:
    -foo
      ↓
    /opt/venv/bin/-foo
Launcher receives:
    $0 = -foo
Prefixing with ./:
    ./$0
      ↓
    /tmp/-foo
```
The launcher was found through `PATH`, but `./$0` points into the current directory instead. The [POSIX command-search rules](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/utilities/V3_chap02.html) don’t guarantee that `$0` contains the resolved pathname.

A few other paths I checked:
- `command -v` works for executable launchers found through `PATH`, but not for sourced activation scripts.
- Generation-time detection can inspect a different `realpath` from the one the launcher later finds through `PATH`.
- Identifying BusyBox by its name, help output, or symlink layout seemed less reliable than checking the behavior directly.

The current version checks whether:
```sh
realpath -- /
```
succeeds and returns `/`. The root directory is always available and resolves to a stable value. Checking both the status and the output also avoids treating BusyBox as compatible if a file named `--` happens to exist, since BusyBox would resolve both `--` and `/`.

It keeps the [`--` end-of-options delimiter](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/V1_chap12.html) when the runtime implementation supports it and falls back when it doesn’t.

The check runs at execution time because the launcher uses whichever `realpath` its environment resolves through `PATH`. In my local benchmark, the extra invocation added about 0.4 ms to each relocatable launcher execution.

I added tests for both branches, including a bare `-foo` operand and the case where a literal file named `--` exists. The full CI run is green.

payload.author: seemethere
payload.body:
We tested this branch (current revision, `1041074`) against a real-world registry pair — Google Artifact Registry + an internal registry — i.e. the enterprise scenario from #6349. One bug and one design gap, both reproducible:

### 1. Silent lockfile corruption when the proxy doesn't preserve artifact paths

GAR restructures file paths (`<name>/<file>` rather than PyPI's `packages/<hashed-dirs>/<file>`). With GAR configured as a PyPI proxy:

```toml
[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "gar-proxy"
url = "https://us-python.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/simple/"
artifact-base-url = "https://us-python.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/"
proxy-for = "pypi"
```

`uv lock` succeeds, but the canonical URLs it derives by base-swap don't exist upstream — the lock records e.g.

```
https://files.pythonhosted.org/packages/idna/idna-3.18.tar.gz   # HTTP 404
```

Installing **through** the proxy works (the reverse mapping round-trips), which means tests that only exercise the proxy path won't catch this. Installing the same lock **without** the proxy — the portability that canonical URLs exist to provide — fails with 404s on the fabricated URLs.

The docs note that path-changing proxies are unsupported, but nothing detects the condition at runtime. Suggestion: hard-error at lock time when a canonical URL can't be derived verifiably, rather than persisting a guess.

### 2. Path preservation excludes the registries this feature seems aimed at

Of the registries we operate against, no two share a path scheme:

| Registry | File path after base |
|---|---|
| PyPI | `packages/<hashed-dirs>/<file>` |
| Google Artifact Registry | `<name>/<file>` |
| our internal registry | `tree/<view>/<name>/<version>/<file>` |

So GAR (and, we suspect, similarly-shaped registries like AWS CodeArtifact) can't participate as either side of a proxy pair under the current design.

A possible fallback when paths don't align: at install-from-lock time, resolve filename→URL via the proxy's simple index page per locked package — lockfile hashes already guarantee integrity regardless of which URL served the bytes. On cost: we measured this exact access pattern against GAR (worst-case index chatter — it serves neither PEP 658 nor PEP 691): **~5s of index fetches for a 235-package lock** at modest parallelism, dwarfed by 4.7GB of wheel downloads.

Happy to test iterations of this branch — we have a production-scale bed for it: two live registries with byte-identical mirrored artifacts and a 799-entry dual-arch lockfile.

Thank you for working on this! I want to report that I tested this locally, and it works great for us.

For context: we have a company-wide PyPI proxy that removes newly published packages (min-release-age < 7). This works in addition to a firewall rule that bans direct access to PyPI. The consequence of this setup is that, the mirror URL always makes into our uv.lock files, and it has been a huge headache for us when working on OSS repositories. We have to configure pre-commit hook that normalize these locks [1][2] and adding instructions in our own AGENTS.md to explicitly handle this as our lock file will change every time we run `uv sync` etc.

The mechanism in this PR is exactly what we need to solve this issue. ❤️
